items.title: Gang Members Violently Murder Christians, Torch Church
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: PRAY.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

At least 47 people and 22 others were injured Sunday night into Monday morning when gang members attacked a church providing shelter to displaced peoples right outside Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

The mayor of Kenscoff, Massillon Jean, said the deadly assault began around 10:30 p.m. and described it as a “night of terror.”

Jean blamed the Viv Ansanm gang coalition, one of the largest groups of violent gang members in Haiti.

According to an official statement, the Haitian government sent reinforcements to help local area police.

“Let there be no mistake: this time of mourning is also a challenge,” said the press release. “And to this challenge, the government responds with the force of law and the legitimate exercise of state force.”

It continued, “All security forces have been placed on maximum alert. Reinforcements are being deployed. The orders are clear: protect, secure, intervene. Government authority will be restored — firmly and without delay — throughout the entire territory of Kenscoff.”

The government added “no armed group will thrive in Haiti” and “[c]riminals will find no truce, no refuge, and no impunity.”

Haitian Bishop Joseph Gontrand Décoste of Jérémie told Aid to the Church in Need (ACN) that churches and Christians as a whole are increasingly the targets of gang violence because believers remain the last stalwart resistance against wrongdoing.

“We are the last remaining bulkhead — moral, ethical, spiritual, and prophetic,” he said. “That is why they want to eliminate us.”

For context, about 40 Catholic parishes have shut down in Port-au-Prince as Christians have faced increasingly deadly violence. In the first seven months of 2026, two priests were abducted and a seminarian was murdered. Last spring, two nuns from the Little Sisters of Saint Thérèse were killed and, in 2024, nine religious sisters, five brothers, and four priests were kidnapped.

ACN has reported gangs control somewhere between 70% and 90% of the capital city of Port-au-Prince.

items.title: The Courage God Gives
items.author: Karen Huang
items.summary:
The CEO was hurting employees with his sharp tongue. No one dared confront him. Everyone was afraid of him, including Gene. But one day the CEO berated a new employee, reducing her to tears. When Gene saw how everyone in the room stayed silent, he spoke up.
“I told him the way he was treating
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

The CEO was hurting employees with his sharp tongue. No one dared confront him. Everyone was afraid of him, including Gene. But one day the CEO berated a new employee, reducing her to tears. When Gene saw how everyone in the room stayed silent, he spoke up.

“I told him the way he was treating people was wrong,” Gene recalls. “He was astonished; it was the first time someone stood up to him. He didn’t change, but I’m glad I spoke up.”

Scripture tells us of another man who stood up to a challenge many were afraid of. Shammah, a military warrior of David, came from difficult circumstances (see 1 Samuel 22:1-2), but God used him to defeat the Philistines, a formidable enemy of the Israelites. “When the Philistines banded together at . . . a field full of lentils, Israel’s troops fled from them” (2 Samuel 23:11). Only Shammah had the courage to defend Israel’s food supply. Being the lone man against the Philistine army meant death, but Shammah “took his stand in the middle of the field. He defended it” (v. 12). 

God helped Shammah defeat the Philistines (v. 12). He may have been the only Israelite in the field, but he wasn’t alone－God was with him, giving him great victory that day. There may be times when we’re called to stand up to a challenge that everyone else is avoiding. Like Shammah, let’s take our stand, relying on God’s presence and help.

Like an unwelcome te
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

In 2018, a man checked into a room at New York hotel for a one-night stay. Remarkably, he used the room for five years without paying another cent—exploiting obscure rent laws to hold on to it. His refusal to leave, however, eventually led to potential prison time for him.

Like an unwelcome tenant who overstays, James warns us that the devil lingers in our lives when left unchecked. “Resist the devil,” James writes, “and he will flee from you” (4:7). The apostle emphasizes that our struggles often come from impure “desires” and “wrong motives” (vv. 1, 3)—things like pride, divided loyalties, and impure thoughts residing in our hearts. To counter such temptation, James offers two commands: “submit . . . to God” and “resist the devil” (v. 7). To submit means surrendering every part of our lives to God. Resisting the devil is equally active, requiring prayer, vigilance, and the wisdom of Scripture.

Like a landlord evicting an unlawful tenant, in God’s strength we can refuse to let the temptation of the devil overtake us. As we resist him, God promises victory as James asserts: “He will flee from you” (v. 7).

When we evict sin and the devil’s influence and “come near to God” (v. 8), we allow His peace, joy, and purpose to dwell more fully in us. The enemy can’t stay where God reigns!

items.title: Tara-Leigh Cobble: Why You Should Stop Treating Your Relationship with God as a Transaction
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Wake up, scroll, maybe crack open a Bible app for five minutes before the day swallows you whole. Whisper a prayer before bed and hope it counts. For a lot of Christians, this is what faith has become: a box to check so you can move on with your day. Tara-Leigh Cobble, creator of The…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Wake up, scroll, maybe crack open a Bible app for five minutes before the day swallows you whole. Whisper a prayer before bed and hope it counts. For a lot of Christians, this is what faith has become: a box to check so you can move on with your day.

Tara-Leigh Cobble, creator of The Bible Recap, used to run her faith the same way.

“I grew up in a space where we’re reading the Bible to find our application point,” she said. “What is my takeaway? What’s my to-do list? How can I be a good Christian? How can I make God happy? Maybe so that God will give me what I want. I viewed it as very transactional.”

The mindset is easy to fall into because it’s how the rest of American life works. Put in the effort, get the payoff. Swipe right, find love. Show up enough Sundays, and God owes you something. Faith, treated this way, stops being a relationship and starts operating like a religious vending machine.

A mentor pushed back on Cobble’s approach years ago. He told her to stop looking for herself when she read the Bible and start looking for God instead. The shift sounds small. Cobble said it changed everything.

“It transforms your relationship with God,” she said. “It takes you from transactional to relational.”

Modern Christian culture doesn’t make that shift easier. Devotionals are curated for speed. Sermons get chopped into one-minute clips built for a feed. Everything is optimized to be quick and digestible, and none of that is built for intimacy.

“Every day we are taking in things that shape our thoughts and that shape our understanding,” Cobble said. “We’re being discipled by all the things around us. And many of those things aren’t telling us the truth.”

TikTok trends, X debates, influencer faith hacks: all of it is shaping belief more than most people want to admit, often faster than a five-minute devotional squeezed between meetings can counter it. Few friendships survive on five minutes a week. Cobble doesn’t think a relationship with God does either.

Her alternative starts with a different question. Instead of reading Scripture to extract a to-do list, read it to learn who God is. Instead of praying for an answer, pray to be with Him. Knowing God, in Cobble’s framing, matters more than performing for Him.

“If your husband only interacted with you for an hour a week, would that feel like intimacy?” she asked. “Would that feel like a rich relationship? No. And yet that’s exactly how many people treat God, checking in on Sunday, maybe sending up a prayer in crisis, but not making Him a daily priority.”

Presence, not obligation, is what deepens faith for Cobble.

“Scripture is the Word of God,” she said. “This is Him revealing Himself to mankind. It’s like being in a conversation with someone you love about who they are, getting to know Him.”

None of that comes naturally to people raised on instant gratification. Seeking God for who He is, rather than what He can produce, means giving up control and sitting with uncertainty. It’s a discipline built through repetition, not a switch that flips once.

Cobble said the payoff shows up in a specific habit her ministry practices daily.

“We end every day of The Bible Recap with what we call the ‘God shot,'” she said. “Our snapshot of God and His character. You don’t leave with a list of dos and don’ts. You leave with a deeper understanding of who He is.”

“You don’t leave The Bible Recap thinking, ‘Today’s assignment is to be nice to people in traffic,'” she said. “Instead, you leave thinking, ‘God is incredibly patient and loving to sinners, including me.’ And that truth sustains you.”

The shift bleeds into how people treat each other. Faith stripped of transaction stops turning relationships into networking opportunities. Generosity replaces self-focus. God’s presence in ordinary moments starts to register instead of getting lost in the noise of religious performance.

That could mean slowing down enough for reflection instead of a rushed reading plan. It could mean praying without an agenda and leaving room for silence. It could mean treating acts of faith as expressions of love rather than boxes to check.

Getting there means unlearning most of what gets marketed as spiritual success. There’s no guaranteed return on investment, no formula, just mystery and waiting without an answer on demand.

Uncomfortable, maybe. But that discomfort is what an actual relationship costs.

items.title: Friday, August 28, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus recognizes the prudence of the five wise virgins.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 1:17-25

For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.

For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written,

“I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,
    and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”

Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, God decided, through the foolishness of our proclamation, to save those who believe. For Jews demand signs and Greeks desire wisdom, but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God’s weakness is stronger than human strength.

Psalm
Psalm 33:1-2, 4-5, 10-11

Rejoice in the Lord, O you righteous.
    Praise befits the upright.
Praise the Lord with the lyre;
    make melody to him with the harp of ten strings.
For the word of the Lord is upright,
    and all his work is done in faithfulness.
He loves righteousness and justice;
    the earth is full of the steadfast love of the Lord.
The Lord brings the counsel of the nations to nothing;
    he frustrates the plans of the peoples.
The counsel of the Lord stands forever,
    the thoughts of his heart to all generations.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 25:1-13

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like this. Ten bridesmaids took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. When the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them; but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. As the bridegroom was delayed, all of them became drowsy and slept. But at midnight there was a shout, ‘Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’ Then all those bridesmaids got up and trimmed their lamps. The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ 9 But the wise replied, ‘No! there will not be enough for you and for us; you had better go to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.’ And while they went to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went with him into the wedding banquet; and the door was shut. Later the other bridesmaids came also, saying, ‘Lord, lord, open to us.’ But he replied, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’ Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus recognizes the prudence of the five wise virgins. In the Middle Ages, prudence was called “the queen of the virtues” because it enabled one to do the right thing in a particular situation. Prudence is a feel for the moral situation, something like the feel that a quarterback has for the playing field or a politician has for the voters in his district.

Wisdom is, like prudence, a kind of vision, but it is, unlike prudence, a sense of the big picture. It is the capacity to survey reality from the vantage point of God, appreciating the grandest perspective. Without wisdom, even the most prudent judgment will be erroneous, shortsighted, and inadequate.

The combination, therefore, of prudence and wisdom is especially powerful. Someone who is both wise and prudent will have both a sense of the big picture and a feel for the particular situation. 

This is the combination possessed by the saints. This is why so many of the saints could be both ethereal and practical. Think of Mother Cabrini—a woman with a remarkably broad vision who was also capable of negotiating with bankers and real estate brokers.

items.title: Apologetics Isn’t Dead, the Sequel: The Conversion of Joe Schmid
items.author: Justin Kalan
items.summary:
Justin Kalan

An important lesson we may gather is that converts beget converts.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Justin Kalan

Four years ago, in my first piece for Evangelization & Culture Online, I discussed the then announced conversion to Catholicism of one of the most popular Christian apologists on Youtube, Cameron Bertuzzi. One of the salient features of Bertuzzi’s conversion was the role that apologetical argument played in it. In particular, Cameron was convinced of the doctrine of the papacy by the biblical typological argument connecting St. Peter with Eliakim, an Old Testament figure mentioned in Isaiah 22. It was Suan Sonna, who also happens to be a convert to Catholicism, whose exposition of this argument helped bring Bertuzzi to Catholicism.

It was a joyous surprise the other day when I found out that Joe Schmid, an agnostic PhD student in philosophy at Princeton and longtime YouTuber, had also converted to Catholicism. 

In one way, Schmid’s conversion is more striking than Bertuzzi’s because he is not merely coming to Catholicism from another Christian denomination but from agnosticism. Though raised Catholic, for years, Schmid has run a very interesting YouTube channel called Majesty of Reason, which focuses on various topics in philosophy, taking particular interest in arguments for and against God’s existence. Indeed, a number of his videos are of him debunking arguments for God’s existence and making arguments against theism and Christianity. 

Schmid outlined his journey from his Catholic upbringing into atheism, agnosticism, and then finally back to the Catholic faith in a video on his channel, and he’ll be appearing on other channels to discuss his conversion as well. Schmid and Bertuzzi both run in some of the same apologetics circles online, and their conversions bear some notable similarities.

Schmid’s Conversion to Theism

Schmid’s conversion followed a logical order, starting with an increasing confidence in God’s existence and then moving towards more specific beliefs in Christianity and finally Catholicism in particular. Schmid notes that during the first few years of his PhD studies, many of his objections to God’s existence, including things like the problem of evil, began to be answered, and many of his previous objections to God’s existence began to fade away. 

For instance, Schmid was impressed by the argument of fine-tuning the universe for life and, more generally, of theism’s broad explanatory power as a simple hypothesis to explain the universe, beauty, our moral intuitions, and many other things. Like Bertuzzi, Schmid was also struck by the immense beauty in the created world that pointed him toward God.

Miracles and the Case for Catholicism

Convinced of theism, Schmid was faced with a variety of evidence for Catholicism during this early period in his PhD program that has played an undersized role in Catholic apologetics in recent years: Catholic miracles. From Eucharistic miracles, to Padre Pio, to Marian apparitions, Schmid was struck by the overwhelming evidence these miracles claim and support, as well as their implications regarding the Catholic faith. 

Schmid’s conversion seems to support a claim Bertuzzi made during a recent Catholic apologetics conference hosted by Trent Horn that miracles are an undertapped source of evidence for Catholicism and should be investigated and shared further. Bertuzzi’s comment has proved prophetic. Just a few weeks ago, Ethan Muse, an up-and-coming Catholic apologist himself and fellow graduate student in philosophy, was on Matt Fradd’s podcast for five hours discussing Catholic miracles, making waves in apologetics circles.

According to Schmid, it was the very same Ethan Muse who routinely took the time to converse with him and share with him the extraordinary evidence for certain Catholic miracles as well as respond to Schmid’s various objections to the Catholic faith toward the end of Schmid’s journey to conversion.

Beyond Argument: The Role of the Saints and Conscience

No conversion consists of an intellectual change alone. Rather, metanoia, or conversion, is a change of the whole person that goes beyond (meta) the mind (nous). A couple of details from Schmid’s account of his conversion reaffirm this truth.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

First, Schmid notes that the powerful story of St. Maria Goretti caused him to seek after the same strong desire for purity and love that she showed in her short life. At the same time, Schmid notes that his conscience began to convict him more and more of his own personal sin and how short he was falling from the life God calls us to. Thus evidence, inspiration from saints, internal witness of conscience, and other religious experiences were all part of what Schmid describes as a “frontal assault” by God against Schmid’s non-belief, which culminated in him going to confession for the first time in many years several months ago and coming back into communion with the Church.

The Upshot

There are a couple lessons that both Bertuzzi and now Schmid’s conversions teach us. First, no one’s conversion (or reversion) to Catholicism is due entirely to apologetic arguments. People are not mere intellects but body and soul creatures with a deep spiritual, emotional, and rational life. As Schmid himself testifies, what drew him back to the Catholic faith was a variety of experiences that God providentially ordered. However, as a philosopher, reason and argument played an indispensable role in Schmid’s conversion just as it did in Bertuzzi’s a few years ago. 

Arguments for God’s existence should be investigated, refined, and utilized in apologetics. This is why Bishop Barron in his introductory lecture at the launch of The New Ressourcement journal noted, “Theologians of a new ressourcement should enter into renewed dialogue with Aquinas precisely on this point of demonstrating God’s existence.” Moreover, arguments for Catholicism, specifically Catholic miracles, can and should be used to demonstrate the truth of the Catholic faith. 

Another lesson we may gather is that converts beget converts. Bertuzzi was deeply impacted by Suan Sonna’s case for Catholicism. Sonna himself was brought into the faith by some of his college friends, some who were themselves converts to Catholicism. Ethan Muse is a recent convert, and he seems to have played a vital role in Schmid’s reversion to Catholicism. This Pauline zeal for the faith demonstrated in these converts helps to power their important ministry in reaching out to nonbelievers who in turn can reach out to others and so forth. The role of one single person can make a remarkable difference not just in another’s life, but indirectly in the lives of all those shaped by that other person too.

What’s Next?

Schmid’s channel’s focus will no longer be philosophy in general but on the case for God’s existence and Catholicism. With Schmid’s intellect and his already impressive résumé, we can expect some great material from him in the future. 

Despite having met Schmid briefly only once and having had only one or two interactions with him online, I cannot overstate how thrilled I am by this news and will continue praying for him on his journey with Christ.
